strengths: Addresses fundamental question about faithfulness of representation intervention in safety alignment, which has been largely assumed but not rigorously questioned
Provides both theoretical contribution (Theorem 3.2 impossibility result for non-linear concept erasure) and practical solution (COCA method with structured reasoning)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 models with multiple attack types, showing substantial improvements (e.g., attack success 71.8% → 17.1% on PAIR)
Strong empirical results while maintaining or improving utility on benign tasks (math reasoning, code generation), unlike some safety methods
Well-designed ablation studies (Figure 3) demonstrating explicit concept reasoning is essential, not just any data augmentation
Clear visualization (Figure 2) showing non-linear separability before COCA and improved linear separability after
Competitive with proprietary models and achieves near-parity with GPT-4o on jailbreak robustness
Practical method that works with existing representation intervention techniques (ReFT, LoFiT) without requiring architectural changes
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Corollary 3.3 assumes explicit dual-head architecture, but practical implementation fine-tunes end-to-end LLMs without this structure. Justification that 'decoder stack implicitly implements concept head' lacks rigorous support

Unclear causal mechanism: Ablation (Figure 3) shows explicit reasoning > fixed concepts, but doesn't isolate whether improvements come from concept concentration versus simply having more detailed training annotations. Missing controlled baseline using equally-detailed non-reasoning data

Equation of faithfulness with robustness is problematic: Improvements could result from better supervised fine-tuning rather than faithful concept localization. No direct validation that harmful concepts are actually erased (e.g., using concept classifiers on representations before/after intervention)

Unfair baseline comparison: COCA uses fundamentally different training data (structured reasoning annotations) compared to vanilla ReFT/LoFiT. Critical missing experiment: fine-tune ReFT/LoFiT on same annotated data without reasoning structure to isolate contribution of method versus data
PCA visualization (Figure 2) shown only at layer 16. To support concept concentration claim, should visualize separability across all layers to show where concentration occurs

Theory-practice gap in Theorem 3.2: While correct, result is somewhat unsurprising from information theory perspective. Practical implications limited since systems don't require perfect erasure, only sufficient robustness
Hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored: No analysis of sensitivity to γ in loss function, prompt phrasing variations, or benign-to-harmful data ratio effects
Over-refusal rates still substantial (~21-23%) without comparison to safety-only fine-tuning baselines to assess trade-offs
Generalization limited to safety alignment: Unclear if COCA works for other concept erasure tasks (debiasing, removing factual knowledge), limiting broader applicability
Teacher model dependency: Relies on GPT-4o for data generation; self-generated variant uses circular process (training model on its own reasoning). Robustness to weaker teachers unexplored

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question about faithfulness of representation intervention for LLM safety
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models, 6 attack types, and both ID/OOD settings with strong empirical results (10.5% avg attack success rate)
Theorem 3.2 provides a formal impossibility result for non-linear concept erasure, correctly showing the fundamental limitation
Extensive ablation studies (Figure 3) clearly demonstrating importance of explicit concept reasoning
Practical method achieves competitive performance with proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5) on attack success rates
Well-written paper with clear presentation and good use of visualizations
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Corollary 3.3 assumes explicit dual-head architecture with specific loss structure, but actual implementation uses end-to-end SFT without maintaining this structure; dismissal of this gap as implicit implementation is insufficiently rigorous

Core claim of 'concept concentration' lacks rigorous validation—only evidence is PCA visualization; missing direct measurements of linear separability, subspace dimensionality, or whether concentration explains improvements

Confounded attribution: unclear whether improvements come from concept concentration mechanism vs. simply using higher-quality GPT-4o-generated training data; self-generated variant (13.2%) performs nearly as well as GPT-4o variant (10.5%)

Limited methodological novelty: COCA is essentially supervised fine-tuning on reasoning-augmented data; reasoning-based safety approaches already explored (SRG, STAIR); structured format is custom but not conceptually novel

Theorem 3.2, while correct, represents a relatively straightforward information-theoretic tautology (cannot erase information while preserving information without distortion); limited depth compared to theoretical standards for ICML

Baseline comparison concerns: ACE achieves suspiciously low 7.3% on GSM8K suggesting implementation issues; Circuit Breaker (RR) produces incoherent outputs—conflating with safety failure is misleading
No human evaluation for safety claims; relies solely on LLaMA-3-Guard (LLM-based judge with potential biases); over-refusal rate remains high at 21.2% (Qwen)
Insufficient failure analysis: doesn't explain why Code attacks remain at 36% success rate; lacks discussion of adaptive attacks targeting structured reasoning format

Reproducibility limited by dependence on proprietary GPT-4o teacher model; self-generated variant performs noticeably worse, suggesting significant contribution from teacher quality rather than mechanism

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 model architectures and 6+ jailbreak attack types with thorough ablations demonstrating the necessity of explicit reasoning
Strong empirical results showing substantial improvements in robustness (e.g., 71.8% → 17.1% on PAIR attack) while maintaining or improving performance on benign tasks

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored question about faithfulness of representation interventions in LLM safety
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (4+), jailbreak benchmarks (ID and OOD), and comparison with numerous baselines
Thorough ablation studies examining importance of explicit reasoning, component contributions, and data volume scaling
Transparent about empirical limitations (e.g., Code Attack vulnerability, high over-refusal rates) and honest about confounding factors
Well-designed presentation with clear figures (Figure 1 motivation, Figure 2 visualizations) and extensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: COCA is fundamentally structured data annotation with reasoning tags—a natural extension of existing reasoning-based safety methods (STAIR, SRG) without clear methodological innovation

Weak theory-practice connection: Theorem 2.2 proves impossibility of perfect erasure but conditions are vaguely defined; Corollary 2.3 assumes dual-head architecture and logistic loss unlike actual LLM training; no rigorous justification for why COCA's structure yields linear concentration

Confounded causal claims: improvements conflate better supervision, reasoning components, and geometric simplification; Table 4's decoupling is insufficient; lacks proper control comparing vanilla improved-SFT without COCA structure
Marginal improvements over baselines: only 1.1% better than STAIR on OOD attacks, within noise margins; unclear when COCA is preferred over existing reasoning-based methods

Unvalidated theoretical claims: linear probe improvements (Table 3) don't validate that concepts are concentrated in a linear subspace; PCA visualizations are 2D projections; no direct evidence of the claimed mechanism

Significant experimental gaps: Code Attack shows 36% ASR (vs <5% elsewhere), revealing vulnerability to concept obfuscation; over-refusal rates 21-26% are substantial; limited to 10K unsafe examples (small for modern standards); requires expensive teacher model annotation
Limited generalization: only tested on safety alignment, not other concept-level interventions; unclear how COCA scales to 70B+ models; structured reasoning may not transfer beyond safety domain

Incomplete comparisons: no comparison with other data-level approaches (adversarial training, explicit jailbreak training); missing analysis of whether gains simply reflect better base model training; insufficient ablations on sensitivity to prompt structure

Presentation issues: heavy notation that obscures rather than clarifies; distinction between 'perfect erasure' (Theorem 2.2) and practical 'robust safety' not clearly articulated; missing mechanistic explanation for why reasoning structure yields linear concentration
Code not available: manuscript states code location as blank; reproducibility compromised despite claims of public release

strengths: Novel theoretical insight: Theorem 2.2 rigorously formalizes why non-linear entanglement makes faithful concept erasure impossible, with clear implications for why existing methods fail

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: 34.5 percentage point reduction in average OOD attack success rate (44.9%→10.4%) on LLaMA-3.1-8B while maintaining or improving performance on math/coding benchmarks across 4 different architectures
Thorough experimental evaluation: 6 OOD attack types + 2 ID attacks, multiple baselines, ablations on data volume/components/reasoning, over-refusal analysis, and comparison with proprietary models

Practical and elegant solution: Data-level approach is simpler than representation interventions, compatible with multiple intervention methods (ReFT, LoFiT), and demonstrates graceful degradation with weaker annotators

Honest treatment of limitations: Transparent discussion of failure modes (adaptive attackers, Code Attack vulnerability), broader impacts, subjective design choices, and acknowledgment that no method is foolproof
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: Corollary 2.3 only guarantees concentration in direction w_c (weaker than full linearity), dual-head model differs from actual autoregressive SFT, and strong assumptions (Gaussianity, isotropy) may not hold; Theorem 2.2 doesn't directly explain why exhaustive position tuning fails

Limited novelty of COCA itself: Method is essentially structured chain-of-thought for safety training—combines existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; while motivation is novel, implementation is straightforward data augmentation

Concerning failure mode inadequately addressed: Code Attack shows 5-7× higher ASR (36-42%) than other attacks despite similar concept identification requirements; explanation via obfuscation lacks strong supporting evidence and deserves deeper investigation

Unclear relationship with related work: COCA, STAIR, and SRG all use reasoning-based supervision; COCA+STAIR combined ablation yields only 4.7% improvement suggesting potential redundancy or that benefits derive from data volume rather than method-specific structure

Practical requirements and costs: Requires teacher model annotations (GPT-4o ~$40 or 30 A100 GPU hours); self-generated variant has 2.8% performance gap; more expensive than vanilla safety training despite some claims of lightweight approach
